raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.title: Two villages cleared for the Raciborz Dolny flood polder
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.place: Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska, gmina Lubomia, Silesian Voivodeship, Poland
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.point: The locality of Nieboczowy in gmina Lubomia, as OpenStreetMap records it. This is the old village site inside the dry polder basin; the replacement village was built about 7 km away near Syrynia, in the same commune.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Odra River Basin Flood Protection Project, P086768, loan IBRD-74360. Approved 21 March 2007, closed 30 June 2020 after a six-year extension. US$184 million committed and US$166.56 million disbursed, against a total project cost of US$1.019 billion; in euros the completion report gives 131.94 million disbursed of an original commitment of 140.1 million, about 91 per cent (completion report, 28 January 2021). The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 June 2021 also rates it Satisfactory.

lenders.name: European Commission
lenders.role: Co-financier through the EU Cohesion Fund. The completion report's cost-overrun table gives 340.56 million euros disbursed at closing against 130 million estimated at appraisal (completion report, 28 January 2021).

lenders.name: Council of Europe Development Bank
lenders.role: Co-financier. The completion report's cost-overrun table gives 204.66 million euros disbursed at closing against 204.9 million estimated at appraisal, and records that the Bank and the Development Bank ran joint project review missions (completion report, 28 January 2021).

companies.name: Regional Authority for Water Management in Gliwice (RZGW Gliwice)
companies.role: State water authority for the upper Odra basin, and the project implementation unit for the Raciborz dry polder and for the resettlement. It later became part of PGW WP, the State Water Holding Polish Waters. The completion report names no construction contractor.

companies.name: Lower Silesian Board for Amelioration and Hydraulic Structures (DZMiUW)
companies.role: The regional water-engineering board for Lower Silesia. The completion report of 28 January 2021 records that the project coordination unit monitored the construction of the new village of Nieboczowy and the process of land acquisition by this board; the report does not say which works that land acquisition was for.

raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.community: The Raciborz Dolny dry polder was built on the land of two villages, Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska. The completion report of 28 January 2021 says the process "included around 700 individuals belonging to about 250 households", and that "aside from the houses, church, and cemetery, all public facilities needed to be relocated". The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 June 2021 gives the same figures: "250 families were resettled, representing about 700 residents". A new village with all services was built for them near Syrynia, about 7 km from the old site. The appraisal document of 21 February 2007 records that the polder needed about 2,600 ha of land, that 20 businesses were in the polder area, most of which would be relocated or closed, and that 22 community assets would be closed or relocated, including a church, a chapel, seven crosses, five wayside shrines, a cemetery, two fire brigade buildings, a kindergarten, a school, a bread house, a recreation room and a sports club. Thirteen wayside shrines and conciliation crosses were moved to the new village. Most houses were bought by agreement over 2003 to 2012: the resettlement plan update of March 2015 counts about 68 buildings acquired by 2006, 1 in 2007, 14 in 2008, 11 in 2009, 8 in 2010, 16 in 2011 and 55 in 2012. In 2013, 30 houses were acquired under an administrative decision of the Silesian Voivodeship of 26 November 2012 rather than by agreement. Opposition was organised and long-running. A Committee for the Defence of Nieboczowy against Displacement was formally constituted in March 2002; the same plan update records 150 appeals against the location permit lodged with the Ministry of Infrastructure and 18 at the Administrative Court in Warsaw, with the Supreme Administrative Court rejecting the complaints on 27 April 2007. A 1998 survey of the two villages found that 91.9 per cent of those surveyed formally accepted displacement; the same plan update records that the survey met hostility and that ten households, 6 per cent, in Nieboczowy refused to answer it. A July 2002 survey of the same population, which followed a campaign by the defence committee urging residents not to co-operate, collected data from 70 per cent of households: 42.2 per cent gave express consent, 8.9 per cent had no opinion and 29.4 per cent refused outright. The same plan update records 74 property owners declaring a will to move in 2007 and 72 families willing to resettle as of April 2010. The completion report says there was "strong initial opposition, even leading to violent resistance", and that the project then built support through consultation; it says the resettled people "have indicated repeatedly that they are content with the new situation", and the Bank presents the resettlement as international best practice. RMF24 reported in April 2007 that about 200 residents were blocking the reservoir and would leave only if the whole village, including the church, was moved with them. The Catholic weekly Gosc Niedzielny reported on 30 June 2020, when the reservoir opened, that Nieboczowy's residents had jointly asked to be relocated and that the new village was built from scratch about 7 km away.
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.displaced_label: people resettled from Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska, about 250 households. The appraisal document of 21 February 2007 gives about 700 people in about 240 to 260 families as the population to be resettled; the completion report of 28 January 2021 carries the same figures and its results annex records the outcome as "All PAP have been resettled (250 families)".
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 689 for this project. That is the appraisal document's own census count of the inhabitants of the two villages, 564 in Nieboczowy and 125 in Ligota Tworkowska, set out in its Annex 10.2 table; the same document rounds it to "about 700 people" in its text and describes the 689 as the "population to be resettled". The 689 and the roughly 700 are the same population counted once and rounded once, not two different quantities. The appraisal table also counts 260 families living in 161 inhabited properties, so the household and family counts in the documents are not interchangeable.
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.killed_note: No death caused by the project or its contractors is recorded in the completion report.
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.outcome: The polder was made operational in January 2020 and the reservoir was formally opened on 30 June 2020. The old village sites are inside the polder basin. The replacement village of Nieboczowy near Syrynia is built and occupied. Both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group rate the project's outcome Satisfactory.

raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.confidence_note: The counts of people and households moved, the village demolition and the 2013 acquisition of 30 houses by administrative decision all come from the lender's own documents and its borrower's resettlement plan, and the figure of about 700 people was already in the appraisal document. Polish press independent of the lender confirms the harm itself: RMF24 on 25 April 2007 reported that 200 residents had blocked construction of the reservoir and would leave only if the whole village, including the church, were moved with them, and Gosc Niedzielny on 30 June 2020 reported from the opening that the villages of Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska lay inside the area the embankments now enclose and that a new Nieboczowy had been built from scratch 7 km away next to Syrynia. The press accounts and the Bank's documents differ in emphasis: the 2020 report says the residents of Nieboczowy jointly demanded the move, while the lender's own completion report records initial opposition that reached violent resistance. No document gives a count of people compelled to move against their will; the 30 houses taken by administrative decision in 2013 is the only compulsion figure in the documents.

hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.title: Shala neighbourhood cleared for lignite mining, and years in temporary housing
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.place: Shala neighbourhood of Hade village, Obiliq municipality, Kosovo
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.point: Hade village, Obiliq municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. The Shala neighbourhood was part of Hade. The resettlement site, Shkabaj or New Hade, is about 8 km east, nearer Pristina.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Energy Sector Clean-up and Land Reclamation Project, P096181, grants IDA-H2340 and IDA-H3190 and credit IDA-52400, with trust funds TF-13509 and TF-90160. Approved 13 June 2006, closed 31 August 2016. The second additional financing, approved 10 May 2013 and filed separately as P131539, added US$4.2 million and created Component F, which paid for monitoring of the Resettlement Action Plan for the Shala neighbourhood. The completion report of 28 February 2017 rates the outcome Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 29 June 2017. The completion report states that the project "did not cause nor finance the resettlement; it only supervised MESP's responsibility to implement the RAP". The Resettlement Action Plan itself was a technical assistance output of another Bank-financed project, the Lignite Power Technical Assistance Project, in 2011.

lenders.name: Netherlands Ministry for Development Cooperation
lenders.role: Co-financier. A grant of US$4.33 million agreed in December 2006 covered the original project's financing gap, and a second grant of US$1.2 million came with the second additional financing (completion report, 28 February 2017).

companies.name: Korporata Energjetike e Kosoves (KEK)
companies.role: Kosovo's energy corporation, which the completion report's abbreviation list writes as "Kosovo Energy Cooperation". It operates the Kosovo A and Kosovo B lignite power plants and the mines that supply them; the project was designed in part to build capacity inside it for clean-up and mining operations. Its mine expansion took the land of the Shala neighbourhood, and it paid the compensation and the temporary rent allowances.

companies.name: Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning of Kosovo (MESP)
companies.role: The ministry responsible for implementing the Shala Resettlement Action Plan, including building the water, sewage and electricity infrastructure at the resettlement site. It ran the grievance commission, which the resettlement completion report says stopped working.

companies.name: rePlan Inc.
companies.role: The international resettlement consultancy commissioned to prepare the Shala Resettlement Action Plan and then, under the Bank-financed Component F, to monitor and report on its implementation.

hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.community: KEK's lignite mine expansion took the Shala neighbourhood of Hade village. The resettlement completion report of July 2016 counts 93 affected households: 63 of them, with 320 full-time residents, were resident households that "needed to be physically displaced", and the other 30 lost land only. By June 2015 the report records 0 of the 63 households still living in Shala. In January 2012, 21 of the 93 households were found to be in a risk zone, were required to leave at once, and were given a monthly rent and living allowance. The Inspection Panel visited the site in 2015 and its Report and Recommendation of 2 September 2015 records residents saying they had been living in temporary housing since 2011 or 2012 because the resettlement site was not ready, and that only in late 2014 did they receive their plots. The same residents told the Panel that the food allowance and emergency rent assistance they had been given during the temporary relocation was discontinued in April 2014 even though the site was not yet ready and many households were still in rented housing. The Panel team recorded its own observations of the incomplete sewerage and the poor condition of the secondary roads at the site. The Bank's completion report says the resettlement was in breach of the Resettlement Action Plan and of the project's legal covenants by December 2013, and that the Bank threatened to suspend disbursements; the breach was resolved when KEK approved more rent payments for the 21 families. The report also records untimely payment of the temporary rent allowances as putting the project in bad standing with its legal covenants. Rebuilding was slow. The resettlement completion report counts 52 of 52 plots allocated with title deeds issued by June 2015, 48 of 52 construction permits issued, 22 plots with construction started or finished, 15 of those 22 houses ready to live in and 12 occupied, with 53 people living at the new site. The same report gives its own explanation for the 30 allocated plots not built on: informal engagements with households revealed that many had opted to stay in the temporary accommodation they had taken in Pristina, while others chose to buy or build elsewhere, and some judged the resettlement site incomplete. Three houses that were ready stood empty in February 2016 because the sewage collecting pipe was blocked. Residents reported 50 metres of blocked sewage pipe in October 2015 and the ministry estimated that about 200 metres needed replacing. Three of the 30 households that lost land only had still not claimed their compensation in February 2016. The 2015 survey ran 32 interviews covering 38 of the 93 affected households, a sample the report puts at 40.8 per cent with a margin of error of 10 points. In it, 43.8 per cent said their economic situation was worse than a year before, against 23.1 per cent in 2011; in the same table the share saying it was better rose from 7.7 per cent to 25 per cent and the share saying it was the same fell from 67.3 to 31.2 per cent. Among the households that lost land without moving, 62.5 per cent said they were worse off, against 37.5 per cent of those physically displaced. The same report concludes that "livelihoods and living conditions have been at least restored and in some instances improved", and that compensation complied with the Bank's resettlement policy. Residents told the Inspection Panel a different story: that compensation was set on a 2004 valuation, that they had to pay the difference between the value of their old plots and the new ones, which they put at about 12,500 euros, that their new plots were smaller, that 20 jobs KEK was to provide under a 2011 agreement had not all materialised, that there was no school or clinic near the site, and that they had never been told of any grievance mechanism.
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.displaced_label: households physically displaced from the Shala neighbourhood, holding 320 full-time residents. The resettlement completion report of July 2016 attributes the 93 affected and 63 physically displaced households to the Shala Resettlement Action Plan as of November 2011, and records the outcome in its own indicator table: 0 of the 63 still residing in Shala as of June 2015.
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 407 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project documents count 93 affected households, of which 63 with 320 full-time residents were physically displaced.
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents or the Inspection Panel report.
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.outcome: The Shala neighbourhood is gone and the mine has expanded over it. The Inspection Panel investigated and its report went to the Bank's board in 2016. The Bank's management agreed to three follow-up actions: repairing a 200-metre section of clogged sewage, technical assistance to revise the resettlement policy framework, and a workshop with the government and KEK. The completion report says the sewage was repaired by December 2016 and the workshop was held on 14 February 2017, and notes that only the sewage repair is directly linked to the project. At the project's closing in August 2016, 12 of the 52 households that chose a plot at the new site were living there. In September 2016 KEK opened negotiations with several hundred more residents who are to be moved for new excavations.

hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.confidence_note: The counts rest on the resettlement completion report that the lender paid for, but the Inspection Panel visited the site, took evidence from residents, recorded observations of its own and published them, and Kosovo press reported on the Panel's investigation. The CEE Bankwatch post of 19 December 2016 is a guest post by Dajana Berisha of the Forum for Civic Initiatives, whom the Requesters designated as their representative to the Panel, so it is a party's account and not an independent one; it gives a third reading of the Panel's finding, that the Bank did not make the resettlement decisions and could not be held directly responsible but could have given specific advice on mitigating the impacts and did not. Prishtina Insight, which saw the leaked investigation report, reported on 14 November 2016 that the Panel found the Bank's management not in compliance with its involuntary resettlement procedures because the resettlement policy framework did not include principles and methods for valuing the assets of people living under the restrictions of the New Mining Field zone, and that the Bank's failings contributed to "real and often severe harm" over a prolonged period. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gives a different account: it says the Panel recognised the Bank's approach and supervision as in compliance, with "two minor instances of non-compliance" over asset valuation, infrastructure delays and malfunctioning sewage, and it sources that statement not to the Panel's report but to management's response to it. The Panel's 2016 investigation report itself was not opened; what was read is the Panel's Report and Recommendation of 2 September 2015, written at the eligibility stage. Both accounts are given here. The lender states that the project did not cause or finance the resettlement and only monitored it, while the resettlement plan it rests on was prepared under a different Bank-financed project. The documents do not agree on how many families had moved in: the resettlement completion report gives 12 of 22 houses occupied as of June 2015, the Panel records the community saying 23 houses built and 11 families moved in during 2015, and Prishtina Insight reported 22 families at the site in November 2016.

tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.title: Motorway built on land whose owners had not been paid
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.place: Tabanovce to Kumanovo, Corridor X, North Macedonia
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.point: Tabanovce, Kumanovo municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. The upgraded section runs 7.3 km from the Tabanovce border crossing to Kumanovo.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Second Trade and Transport Facilitation Project, P091723, loan IBRD-48590. Approved 29 May 2007, closed 30 June 2012 after a nine-month extension of an original closing date of 30 September 2011. Loan of 15 million euros, equivalent to US$20 million; the completion report's data sheet gives US$20.52 million disbursed, while the Independent Evaluation Group's review gives US$20.27 million in its loan column. Environmental category B. In March 2009 the Bank's team found that compensation for the road upgrade had not been paid to all landowners before the contractor started work, and the Bank sent a Warning of Suspension of Disbursement for the part of the loan covering the road upgrade. The completion report of 12 December 2012 rates the outcome Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 September 2013, which rates overall Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory against the report's Satisfactory.

companies.name: Agency for State Roads
companies.role: The national road agency and the implementing body for the road upgrade, including land acquisition and compensation payments; its Director was the project coordinator. The revised resettlement plan required it to hold the full assessed compensation in a special account. The completion report names no construction contractor, referring only to "the contractor".

companies.name: Customs Administration
companies.role: A unit of the Ministry of Finance, and the implementing body for the Blace border crossing component, where 27 parcels of land had to be acquired that the government had told the Bank would not be needed.

tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.community: Land was taken for the 7.3 km upgrade of the Tabanovce to Kumanovo section of Corridor X to motorway standard. The completion report of 12 December 2012 records "about 102 affected owners involving about 294 parcels of land". In March 2009 the Bank's team found that compensation for that land "was not paid to all landowners prior to start of works by the contractor", contrary to the Resettlement Action Plan and the loan agreement, because some owners had gone to court to raise the amounts. The report calls the delays in payment "a serious safeguard violation which were corrected in time and detracted slightly from the very positive outcome". The Bank sent a Warning of Suspension of Disbursement for the road part of the loan. The warning was lifted a few months later when the Bank and the government agreed to amend the plan and the loan agreement so that works could proceed as long as money for compensation was set aside in the road agency's budget; the national law was changed in the same direction. Four or five court cases were still open when the project closed; the report says they have since been decided, and that under Macedonian law payment from the state budget follows automatically once a court makes an award. At the Blace crossing to Kosovo, the government assured the Bank during preparation that no land acquisition was needed; at implementation 27 parcels had to be acquired, and the completion report says this held up the start of civil works for more than two years. The report says 102 households were expected to lose part of their land holdings and that no residence was affected; the resettlement plan of 5 April 2007 says there would be no physical displacement of persons and no buildings to demolish.
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 294 for this project. The documents do not agree on what 294 counts. The appraisal document of 16 April 2007 says there are 294 agricultural plots to be acquired affecting 102 owners, and the completion report of 12 December 2012 says there were "about 102 affected owners involving about 294 parcels of land". The resettlement plan of 5 April 2007 says instead that "there are 294 owners affected by the Project". Both readings are given here. No project document records anyone being relocated.
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents.
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.outcome: The motorway is open and the completion report says all land acquisition cases have been resolved. The safeguard violation is recorded in both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review; the review says it was "quickly" addressed. No independent record of how much the owners who went to court were finally paid was found.

It is still a lender reporting on its own project: no court record, audit or news report about the affected owners was found, and the documents give no figure for how much any owner was eventually paid, nor how long any owner waited.

igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.title: A road worker killed and a resident's house damaged on the Igoeti highway works
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.place: Igoeti village, Kaspi municipality, Shida Kartli, Georgia
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.point: Igoeti village, Kaspi municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. The project upgraded the 24 km of the E60 highway from Igoeti to Sveneti and built the Igoeti bypass and its four bridges.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second East-West Highway Improvement Project, P094044, credits IDA-43730 and IDA-45120. Approved 18 December 2007, closed 30 June 2012. XDR 34.72 million disbursed. The completion report of 28 December 2012 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 October 2013.

companies.name: Roads Department of Georgia
companies.role: The national road agency, moved in the 2009 ministerial reforms from the Ministry of Economic Development to the new Ministry of Regional Development and Infrastructure, and the project's implementing agency. Its Resettlement Unit, four staff plus a hired consultant, handled land acquisition and compensation. The completion report does not name the construction contractors, calling them "the first road contractor" and the contractor hired in June 2011.

igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.community: One of the first road contractor's local employees was killed while performing a pavement test on the project section. The completion report of 28 December 2012 says he was "killed by a speeding car whose driver ignored a road construction warning sign", and that the contractor "refused to pay compensation to the victim's family for about 1.5 years, despite constant reminders by the Bank Team" and the Roads Department. The report's lessons section says the accident shows that traffic safety during road construction works remains a problem, and that payment to a contractor should be refused where it has not met safety requirements. The same contractor started civil works before land acquisition from a resident of Igoeti village was officially completed, and in doing so damaged her house and made improper use of her land. That case stayed open from 2009 until 25 June 2012, when she signed an agreement accepting GEL 11,139, about US$6,700, for 954 square metres of land and 62 fruit trees; payment took effect on 9 July 2012. She had already been paid GEL 45,000, about US$27,270, in February 2011 for damage to her summer house during construction. The report says the first contractor's work was unsatisfactory in many instances, that it knew of design errors and "took advantage of the situation", and that it failed to comply with the environmental management plan, especially on storage and disposal of materials. Land take ran well beyond the original plan: the original resettlement plan envisioned 167 land plots covering 91,968 square metres on the Igoeti to Sveneti section, and the number of plots actually affected within the right of way of the main alignment reached 192, covering 146,914 square metres. The completion report attributes the difference to inconsistent right-of-way data and poor coordination between the cadastral data in the plan and the data used in the preliminary design. About 4 more hectares of private land were needed for connecting roads to neighbouring villages. The completion report says all compensation was paid by the end of the project, totalling GEL 1,343,773, about US$0.81 million, and that all outstanding cases were resolved to the satisfaction of the affected people.
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.killed_note: One local employee of the first road contractor was killed on the project section while performing a pavement test. The completion report of 28 December 2012 says he was "killed by a speeding car whose driver ignored a road construction warning sign", calls it "the fatal accident on the Project section", and draws the lesson that traffic safety during construction works on roads remains a problem and that payment should be refused to a contractor found not to have complied with safety requirements. The cause the document gives ties the death to the works, so it is counted. The worker is not named and the report gives no date for the accident.
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 607 for this project. No project document records anyone being relocated: the appraisal document said no physical relocation was expected, and the completion report records land and tree compensation only.
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.outcome: The highway section is built. The first contractor's contract was allowed to expire and another contractor was hired in June 2011 to finish the works and repair the defective ones. The family of the dead worker was paid after about a year and a half, according to the completion report, which does not give the amount. The Igoeti land case closed with payment in July 2012.

ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.title: Farm land taken for drainage works before the resettlement plan covered it
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.place: Bagdad, Rishtan and Altiaryk districts, Fergana region, Uzbekistan
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.point: Bagdad (Bog'dod) town, Bagdad district, Fergana region, as OpenStreetMap records it. Bagdad is one of the three districts where land was taken; the project area covers about 67,000 ha across the three.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Ferghana Valley Water Resources Management Project Phase I, P110538, credit IDA-46480. Approved 24 September 2009, closed 31 December 2016. XDR 33.76 million disbursed. The safeguards compliance rating was downgraded during implementation over the land acquisition and later upgraded. The completion report of 16 May 2017 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 16 October 2017.

companies.name: Projects Implementation Unit for Water Infrastructure, Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources of Uzbekistan
companies.role: The unit inside the national water ministry that ran the project, prepared the resettlement plans and the land acquisition reports, and operated the grievance mechanism. Compensation amounts were set by decisions of the Fergana regional governor (khakim) and the district governors.

ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.community: Rehabilitating drainage and irrigation canals took farm land, permanently and temporarily, and removed trees along roads, canals and drains. The resettlement plan prepared before appraisal and updated in 2011 covered 37 farmers. The completion report of 16 May 2017 says that "between 2012 and 2014, 338 farmers were affected by the project activities, and land acquisition took place without the RAP being updated, which constituted a noncompliance with the World Bank OP 4.12", because local authorities would not approve updates until the list of farmers was final. The report also says that "compensation payments were done with delay after land acquisition and/or civil works started", blaming invalid bank details and suspended bank accounts, and that "in most cases, the PAPs did not receive any cash as compensation was used to settle outstanding tax arrears". It adds that some farmers who were paid turned out not to be affected at all, and that there was no mechanism to recover those payments. The borrower's own report on land acquisition in 2012 to 2014, dated November 2015, puts figures to it and explains most of the gaps. Four decisions of the Fergana regional governor between October 2011 and April 2014 covered 513 farm enterprises in all. Under the first, of 10 October 2011, all 37 enterprises listed were paid in full. Under the decision of 13 December 2013, damage to 189 enterprises was assessed at UZS 611,791,000 and UZS 512,663,126 was paid to 155 of them; of the 34 unpaid, 10 had suffered no damage because part of the collector works was dropped at detailed design, and the money for the remaining 24 came back because their bank details were wrong. Under the decision of 15 February 2014, the report's text says damage to 62 enterprises was assessed at UZS 127,215,230 and UZS 126,246,030 was paid to 60 of them, the other two held up by incorrect bank accounts, while the report's own summary table lists 128 enterprises under the same decision with 60 paid; both readings are in the one document. Under the decision of 15 April 2014, the text says UZS 235,988,691 was paid to 121 land users and that of the remaining 38, 28 had suffered no damage during construction and 10 had money returned over bank details, while the summary table gives 123 paid. The table's total is 373 paid of 513, and the report accounts for the 140 difference as 36 farmers awaiting correct banking details and 104 farmers who were not harmed because the work was done before planting and after harvest; the table's own rows sum to 375 rather than 373. A further decision of 25 December 2014 assessed damage of UZS 494,989,548 and the report says no payment had been made under it because funds had to be reallocated. The report puts total damage under the project at UZS 1,918 million, of which UZS 937,803,509 was paid in 2011 to 2014 and UZS 980,473,630 was still to be paid by the end of 2015, a balance that includes the UZS 436.35 million it estimates for 2015 and not only arrears to the farmers already assessed. Land taken ran 515.25 ha in 2012 and 197.49 ha in 2015; for 2013 the report's text gives 358 ha while its table for the same year totals 334.51 ha, and for 2014 it gives 334.52 ha under one contract and a further 226.57 ha under another. The completion report says all outstanding payments were made before the project closed, and that the use of compensation against tax arrears "did not seem to cause any unhappiness in the farmers' community".
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 263 for this project. No project document records anyone being relocated; the figures in the documents count farmers and farm enterprises whose land was taken, not people moved.
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents.
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.outcome: The drainage works were built and the project closed in December 2016 with the outstanding compensation paid, according to the completion report. The Independent Evaluation Group's field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 March 2019 records both sides of the compliance question: its safeguards section says "overall, the project complied with the implementation of safeguards" and that "previous reviews of the safeguards confirmed full compliance", while its assessment of the implementing agency says the project unit was understaffed for environmental and social safeguards, which "partly led to noncompliance with both", and that issues over approval of the resettlement action plan and delays in compensation payments to project-affected people "persisted for some time, causing the downgrade in safeguards performance ratings".

ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the lender and its borrower. No Uzbek press report, court record or audit about these farmers was found, and in Uzbekistan in those years an independent account would be hard to produce. The borrower's report disagrees with itself in several places, as set out above, and those figures are left as the document gives them. The lender's own documents cut both ways on the harm: the completion report records compensation paid late after works started and used to settle tax arrears, and the assessment report records both full compliance and non-compliance in the same document. The unpaid balance of UZS 980,473,630 is as recorded in November 2015 and covers assessed and expected damage together; the completion report says all outstanding payments were made before closing but gives no final figure, so how long any individual farmer waited cannot be stated.

yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.drop_reason: The lender's own outcome documents say the works that took the land were not financed by the project, and the project's own land take exists only as a plan. The completion report of 3 December 2015, paragraph 33, says: "During the course of project implementation, the need for land acquisition arose at passing loops and near Yenice Logistic Village (which was not financed by the Bank but adjacent to the project)." The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 June 2016 repeats that clause and cites it to page 9 of the completion report, so it is the report's statement and not a separate finding. The appraisal document of 12 May 2005 did not trigger the involuntary resettlement policy and says "no resettlement or land acquisition is involved". The actual, past harm in the file is the urgent expropriation at Yenice: the resettlement plan of March 2011 records that TCDD's executive board decided on 25 January 2008 to expropriate about 277,249.71 square metres at the Yenice terminal for a logistics village, that a Council of Ministers decree of 31 March 2008 authorised urgent expropriation under Article 27, that the Tarsus courts set the value of 155 parcels at TRY 17,977,032.97, that TCDD valued 47 private parcels covering 220,553.71 square metres at TRY 5,620,188.46, that four owners settled at the June 2010 meeting, that TRY 5,308,128.58 set by the courts was remitted on 30 June 2010 into accounts opened in the parcel owners' names before the courts granted entry, and that valuation lawsuits were filed on 14 July 2010 for the 43 parcels where no agreement was reached. All of that predates the 2011 restructuring by which the Bank first brought Yenice inside a resettlement plan, and none of it is on works the loan financed. The land take for the project's own works is plan-level only: 74 parcels totalling 302,388.16 square metres at an estimated TRY 9.2 million, 41 households losing land, three households whose houses would be affected. Checked in the outcome documents: paragraphs 16 and 33 of the completion report, its results framework, and the safeguards section of the review. Neither records any land acquired, any household paid, or how the 43 court cases ended, and no Turkish court record or news report of the Yenice expropriations was found. The drop turns on the lender-link test and not on the forward rule; if a document is ever found tying the loan to the Yenice land take, or recording how the 43 valuation suits ended, the row is worth reopening. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 256.

dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.community: Three sub-projects moved people or interrupted their livelihoods: Dartlo, a protected village high in Tusheti, and the towns of Telavi and Kvareli. The completion report of 18 June 2018 says the Kvareli plan covered temporary income losses of 33 people, the Telavi plan covered temporary relocation and business interruption for 91 households and 84 businesses, and the Dartlo plan covered 44 residential buildings whose owners had to move out for the duration of the works. The same paragraph says both the Kvareli and the Telavi plans "were fully implemented prior to the start of physical works". The resettlement plan update for Dartlo, dated July 2016, records what happened in the first season. Rehabilitation works started on 33 buildings in 2012. All 33 fell in the category whose residents had to move out for the works, but the update records that seven of them were ruins and that seven more had only small-scale works which the building and supervisory company said needed no temporary relocation, leaving the owners of 19 buildings entitled to compensation under the 2012 plan. "In 2012, no one owner of the buildings has received the compensations." Compensation due for 2012 to 21 affected persons was paid in 2014 to 19 of them, and two were still waiting, with payment planned for 2016 once the plan was updated. The same update counts the entitled owners as 19 in one passage and the persons due payment as 21 in another. The update also records that in 2012 none of the buildings was officially registered and owners were identified from villagers' verbal statements, which later changed who was entitled: one building recorded as having a single owner turned out to have three. At Telavi, the completion report says 37 grievances submitted in 2014 were not addressed until 2016. A footnote says those grievances "involved claims by affected business owners that the provided compensation did not fully cover losses incurred as a result of the Project". An independent consultant was appointed in the summer of 2014 to help settle them and to check whether compensation had been paid in line with Bank policy; the report says the assessment helped address the complaints and "confirmed compliance". Separately, the report records that for an extended period environmental supervision and reporting were poor, "creating substantial risks for the livelihood of affected communities, health of workers": construction companies operated without adequate arrangements for waste disposal, and there were "obvious deficiencies in protecting workers' health and safety as well as in managing disturbance of communities residing in and around work sites". The completion report says the project was compliant with the resettlement policy, that all complaints were addressed, and that the Dartlo plan was completed without grievances or complaints.
dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 165 for this project. No document records a permanent relocation. The counts in the documents are of plan coverage for temporary moves and business interruption: 91 households and 84 businesses at Telavi, 44 residential buildings at Dartlo, 33 people at Kvareli.
dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents. The completion report records deficiencies in protecting workers' health and safety but no injury count.
dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.outcome: The works are finished and the project closed at the end of 2017. By the July 2016 plan update, two of the Dartlo owners due compensation for 2012 had still not been paid, four years after the works on their houses. The Telavi grievances were settled in 2016 and the lender's assessment found compensation had complied with its policy. No independent account of the Dartlo or Telavi compensation was found.

dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.confidence_note: The late payments at Dartlo and the two-year delay in answering the Telavi grievances are stated in the lender's own documents, one of them the borrower's plan update. Searches in Georgian for press or official accounts of the Telavi business compensation found nothing. The lender's conclusion cuts the other way on both counts: it says the project complied with the resettlement policy, that all complaints were addressed, and that Dartlo was completed without grievances. The numbers are small and the moves were temporary.

moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.drop_reason: The outcome document's whole quantitative content is a count of people affected, and it records that nobody moved and everybody was paid. The completion report of 30 October 2013, in its involuntary resettlement section, says KEGOC "acquired about 14 hectares of land for permanent use and 555 hectares for temporary use", that "in total, 316 persons (land users) have been affected. None had to be resettled, and all received reasonable cash compensation", and that "all compensation has been completed prior to loan closure". The finding it does make is procedural: "construction of the line started prior to the Bank's formal approval of a Land Acquisition Plan", after which a plan was approved with "relevant retroactive measures" to bring compensation into line with the resettlement policy. ICIJ's 316 is that affected count. That leaves neither limb of the forward rule: no relocation, and no loss recorded to any identified person. This is the same shape as four rows dropped in this batch, including Talimarjan and Kakheti, where land was taken, everyone was paid and no complaint was recorded. Checked in the outcome documents: the safeguards section and the Bank-performance section of the completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 June 2014. One route back is the Land Acquisition Plan itself, which carries no date on its cover and gives its figures as of May 2012: its Table 2.2 breaks the 316 into 222 land users in Enbekshikazakh, 58 in Ili, 20 in Raimbek, 13 in Talgar and 3 in Kapshagai town, with a footnote that "compensation payment agreements are under conclusion", and its Appendix 2 lists each land user by name with the area taken, the compensation amount and dates in 2011 and 2012. If those date columns can be read cleanly they may show land taken months before agreement for named people, which would be a documented harm; in the harvested text the table's columns are mangled and no such claim can be made from it. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 316.

osh-batken-isfana-road-no-land-taken.drop_reason: The outcome document records no land taken and nobody moved. The completion report of 27 June 2015, paragraph 2.4.7, states: "There was no land acquisition under either the parent project or AFs, and there were no project affected people (PAPs) under the parent project and AF1. The total compensation of about KGS 350,000 (US$7,000) was paid to seven project affected businesses under AF2." Those seven are road-side businesses at the Nookat pass, compensated for profit lost during construction; the borrower's own section of the same report confirms the government issued a decree in March 2013 to release the money and that the plan was translated into Kyrgyz and presented to the seven. Neither limb of the forward rule is met: no relocation count, and no harm left standing after payment. Checked in the outcome document: paragraphs 2.4.4 to 2.4.8 on social safeguards, the results framework, and the borrower's completion contribution. The brief's harm hits were context, not project harm. Its two 'count with a relocation verb' sentences were the June 2010 civil unrest in Osh and Jalal-Abad, in which about 400,000 people were displaced, which the report gives as a reason for implementation delay, and the resettlement framework's recital of the policy threshold of 200 displaced people. Its 'arrests, police or force' sentence was a dispute between the Ministry of Transport and the Ministry of Internal Affairs over who owned the road safety strategy, and its death sentences were road fatality rate indicators. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 32.

bishkek-osh-urban-infrastructure-nine-af.drop_reason: The outcome document counts nine affected people in total and records each of them paid. The completion report of 26 May 2016, paragraph 38, says four resettlement action plans were prepared, for Bash-Karasuu, Naryn, Isfana and Tash-Kumyr, that "there were nine project affected people", and that only one complaint was received, addressed at the first grievance stage. Its borrower annex itemises the payments: five farmers in Orok ayil aymak received KGS 240,000 between them; a Naryn resident received KGS 25,000 for the loss of a partially constructed house plus a land plot from the mayor's office; an Isfana farmer received KGS 28,820 and a land plot; two Tash-Kumyr residents were paid KGS 6,000 each for removed trees. Neither limb is met: nobody was relocated, and no compensation is recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome document: the safeguards paragraphs, the grievance record and the borrower's social safeguards annex. The brief's 'compensation unpaid or late' hit was a June 2014 meeting with the Osh vice-mayor at which two Tash-Kumyr residents agreed a water main route through their orchards and were given an explanation about outstanding amounts; the relevant plan budgets 12,200 som for four years of apricot crop and saplings, and the completion report records the payment made. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 9.

armenia-electricity-supply-reliability-n.drop_reason: No outcome document counts land taken, households affected, or compensation left unpaid, and the harm language in the documents has delay to the works as its stated consequence. The completion report of 30 July 2024 says the utility's financial constraints "contributed to the documented delays, including those related to land acquisition and RAP compensations", and the next sentences give the consequence: the transmission rehabilitation finished in 2020, four years after the original closing date. Its social safeguards section says compliance was rated Satisfactory at closing, that all compliance reports found the abbreviated resettlement plans complied with the framework and national law, and that "most of the affected households (on average from 80 to 95 percent) were satisfied" with valuation, the size of compensation and the payment process. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 15 January 2025 repeats the 80 to 95 per cent. Neither limb is met. Checked in the outcome document: the social safeguards section, the factors affecting implementation, and the grievance record, which gives a garbled count of 157 grievances received and addressed. The resettlement policy framework of July 2015 says only that "it is expected that the number of persons to be relocated is minimal", a plan sentence with no outcome behind it. The brief's four harm hits were all recitals in the framework: the rule allowing possession before payment where compensation is pledged in court, the definition of replacement cost, the court deposit procedure, and the audit clause about livelihood restoration. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 440.

kakheti-regional-roads-31-plots-paid.drop_reason: Two outcome documents agree that the land taken was smaller than planned and that every owner was paid without complaint. The Independent Evaluation Group's field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 17 June 2020 says the road department "completed the land acquisition for the section between Vaziani and Gombori in 2010 and for the section between Gombori and Telavi in 2012", that design changes meant "the land acquisition involved 31 land plots instead of the 174 expected at appraisal", and that the department "fully compensated all landowners in accordance with the provisions of the resettlement action plan and received no complaints". The review of 10 June 2016 gives the same 31 against 174 and the same conclusion. Neither limb is met: no relocation, and no compensation recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome documents: the social safeguards sections of both, and the assessment report's appendix B. A trap worth recording: the assessment report covers two projects, and the paragraph beginning "At appraisal, no land acquisition or resettlements were envisioned... Minor land acquisitions had to take place during project implementation" sits under the heading for the Secondary and Local Roads Project, P086277, not for this one. The brief's harm hits were road-safety fatality indicators and the entitlement matrix's recital of compensation at replacement cost. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 422.

kyrgyz-second-rural-water-118-paid.drop_reason: The outcome document counts 118 affected people, mostly temporary, and records all of them paid. The completion report of 27 April 2015, paragraph 46, says the resettlement policy was triggered during implementation, that "118 Project Affected Persons (PAPs) in ten villages were identified", that they were "mainly affected by temporary restrictions to access or loss of trees and crops", and that "all PAPs were fully paid by the project closing date", with compensation of KGS 1,979,254, about US$50,000, paid exceptionally out of the credit itself. Neither limb is met. Checked in the outcome document: the safeguards section, the borrower's resettlement annex listing the ten villages, and the sections on the suspended sub-projects. One finding for another round rather than this row: the same report records that water schemes failed in 26 villages, and works were suspended before completion in Korumdu, Temir and Chelpek, under the predecessor Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Project, not under this one, "mostly associated with poor design of the water sources under the RWSSP", and that this project had to go back and fix them, deferring US$1.5 million of service work at Chelpek. The brief's harm hits were all framework recitals on eligibility and replacement cost. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 245.

albania-water-sector-resettlement-avoide.drop_reason: The outcome document says the project avoided resettlement and gives no count of land taken or compensation unpaid. The completion report of 25 September 2020, paragraph 56, says the late appointment of the social safeguards specialist "caused delays in implementing the social safeguard instruments (for example, the RAP), which resulted in changing the locations of one of the wells as the implementation of the RAP was stalled", and that "the project avoided resettlement by changing the routes of some of the water and wastewater lines in some areas". Checked in the outcome document: paragraphs 55 and 56 on safeguards and the grievance record. The resettlement plan of January 2013 is plan-level only: 28 land owners along the new pipeline across four communes, with compensation estimated at 4,246,330 lek, about US$40,442, and a statement that no owner would be fully expropriated. talimarjan-transmission-land-compensatio.drop_reason: The outcome document records land taken from leasehold farms with compensation completed and no complaints. The completion report of 22 December 2016, paragraphs 50 to 52, says the project needed about 12.03 ha permanently and 159.42 ha temporarily from 114 leasehold farms in Kashkadarya and Samarkand, 90 in the first and 24 in the second; that "in total 141 farmers and Hokimiyats in eight districts... received compensation"; that land acquisition and compensation payments were "completed by April 2013"; that apart from 26.7 ha for the substation the takes averaged 1.1 ha; and that "to date, no complaints have been recorded". It explains the shifting counts, 114 in the plan, 147 in a supervision aide memoire, 141 in the final list, by a government farm-consolidation programme and by an audit that found six farmers had been paid in error and asked them to return the money, and says the entitlement matrix was never modified. Neither limb is met: nobody was relocated and no compensation is recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome document: the involuntary resettlement paragraphs, the borrower's section, which says "land compensations have been paid during 2010-2013", and the social impact discussion. The brief's harm hits were monitoring-indicator headings in the resettlement plan of September 2010 that list "number of people not receiving compensation in time" as a thing to be measured, and a risk-matrix row in the appraisal document naming non-compliance as a risk to be managed.
